extracted.intended_audience: public relations professionals and nonprofit/organizational communicators (social media managers, communications directors)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for nonprofit/organizational social media practice: monitoring conversations, engaging influencers, running disaster-focused channels, measuring sentiment, and shifting internal culture to integrate new media into public relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proactive social media monitoring
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish an online monitoring process to review what people are writing and saying via social media so criticism can be discovered early rather than being surprised by it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After Katrina the Red Cross hired a new media specialist whose first goal was to study online conversations. Use search engines and social media sites (Technorati, Google, online forums, Facebook, Flickr) to find posts and read entries daily. Monitoring should reveal both negative and positive comments and enable early intervention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-way communication and direct response
rubrics_metrics.description: Use social media as a two-way channel to respond directly to misinformation and stakeholder concerns rather than relying solely on traditional media broadcasts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respond and correct the record online; introduce yourself in outreach (example: 'Hi this is Wendy from the American Red Cross…'). Each comment is an opportunity to build a relationship; work with internal colleagues to address issues raised and follow up when resolved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and engage key influencers
rubrics_metrics.description: Monitor conversations to discover influencers in online communities and proactively reach out to them to build relationships and amplify accurate information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tools like Technorati to find blogs but evaluate influence by content and passion as well as ranking. Read entries from low-ranked blogs because 'posts with just two links have the best stories.' Reach out to bloggers who have firsthand experience (e.g., blood donors) — they can inspire peers to act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure sentiment and surface trends (metrics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tag and analyze online conversations to surface trends and themes that show what the public actually cares about, informing organizational priorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat conversations as raw data: tag posts, come up with trends and themes, and report those findings. Use social bookmarking (del.icio.us) to collect important posts and to enable trend analysis across entries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness and rapid reaction time
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that social media requires an even faster reaction time than traditional media cycles; the public expects immediate answers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be prepared to respond within hours or days. Use quick channels (e.g., Twitter) to provide immediate updates such as shelter locations and to accept short status updates for systems like 'Safe and Well.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform-specific tactics (blogs, Twitter, Flickr, Facebook)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use each social media technology according to its strengths — blogs for richer updates, Twitter for short alerts, Flickr for compelling photos, Facebook for groups and community connections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: create disaster blogs and RSS feeds; Twitter emergency alerts and Safe and Well status updates; Flickr campaigns (tagged photos) to engage stakeholders; maintain and monitor Facebook groups and causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create disaster-specific portals and aggregate feeds
rubrics_metrics.description: Set up centralized disaster portals that aggregate local chapter feeds and provide a single hub for disaster-focused information and RSS feeds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: redcross.wordpress.com as a disaster portal where chapter or disaster-generated blogs are aggregated. For large disasters, bring in volunteers to update the portal rather than relying solely on individual chapters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empower local chapters while centralizing support
rubrics_metrics.description: Allow individual chapters to generate local content (blogs, updates) but provide national-level aggregation, technical support, and coordination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local chapters may run their own blogs (examples provided). The national office helps with web support and can mobilize volunteers to update aggregated feeds during large-scale events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build community spaces to encourage storytelling
rubrics_metrics.description: Create community-oriented blogs and groups that invite stakeholders to tell their stories and share photos to foster connection and advocacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a 'Red Cross Chat' blog as a community space and a Flickr group for sharing photographs. Campaigns (e.g., Malaria Awareness Day with tagged photos) can encourage participation and peer-to-peer support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Designate a dedicated new media specialist/role
rubrics_metrics.description: Assign or hire a staff member responsible for monitoring, engaging, identifying influencers, and coordinating social media initiatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wendy Harman (Senior Associate, New Media Integration) monitored conversations, responded to bloggers, identified influencers, and developed internal education — illustrating the responsibilities and impact of the role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal education and culture shift
rubrics_metrics.description: Educate employees about the value and norms of social media to achieve an organizational culture that listens and engages with stakeholders online.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop internal presentations and training to show how social media differs from traditional communications; emphasize that stakeholders have a voice online and staff must learn to communicate in that environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage stakeholder passion over raw ranking
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess influence not just by quantitative rankings but by stakeholder passion and the quality of stories shared, which can have outsized influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure passion qualitatively (personal stories, donations, volunteer experiences). Passion can drive influence regardless of an authority ranking; passionate donors/bloggers often inspire peers to act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Run proactive campaigns and act as the hub
rubrics_metrics.description: Use social media proactively — run planned campaigns and position organizational channels as a paced hub that coordinates initiatives and amplifies stakeholder activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate new media into annual campaigns (podcasts, videos, photos, text). The organization should both respond to conversations and proactively seed campaigns that engage stakeholders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use tagging and social bookmarking for tracking
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply consistent tagging and social bookmarking practices to collect, organize, and later analyze important blog posts and social content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: tagging important posts on del.icio.us (del.icio.us/AmericanRedCross) and using Flickr photo tags to gather campaign content; tagging supports trend identification and aggregation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitor and amplify positive commentary as well as negative
rubrics_metrics.description: Track positive mentions and praise in social media and engage those authors to amplify support and strengthen relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitoring revealed many positive comments; outreach and small gestures often led bloggers to write appreciative follow-ups, creating additional positive entries that can be amplified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't rely solely on automated authority metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat automated rankings (e.g., Technorati Authority) as one input but not the sole determinant of influence or importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Red Cross reads posts across the spectrum (from authority ranking of zero to 30,000+) because lower-ranked posts can contain powerful, influential stories. Combine metrics with qualitative reading.
